extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, students of drama and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating tragic drama (plot, character, discovery, diction, spectacle, chorus, and staging), drawn from Aristotle's Poetics. Emphasises cause-and-effect, probability, and theatrical effect in tragedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot: reversal and discovery (complex plot)
rubrics_metrics.description: The best (complex) plots turn on reversal (peripeteia) and discovery (anagnorisis); the reversal and discovery should arise from the plot itself rather than be mechanically produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Sophocles' Oedipus (discovery by incidents) is ideal. Anti-patterns: revelations manufactured by the poet (e.g., scenes made merely to 'prove the point') are inartistic. The complex plot (reversal+discovery) is the chief species of tragic plot and produces the strongest tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of discovery and their artistic merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery scenes occur by tokens, by manufactured declaration, by memory/distress, or by inference; their artistic value differs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ranking given: best are discoveries produced directly by incidents (surprising but likely), next those from inference, then those from memory/distress, and lastly token-based or poet-manufactured discoveries. Anti-patterns: discovery 'manufactured by the poet' or constructed 'to prove the point' is inartistic; tokens (birthmarks, wounds, necklaces) are the least artistic though can be used well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incidents must be inevitable or probable (causal coherence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Incidents and the chain of events should be such that it is inevitable or at least probable that one thing follows another; the dénouement should be the result of the plot itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There must be nothing inexplicable within the play; if anything inexplicable appears, it must lie outside the tragedy. Avoid arbitrary interventions that do not follow logically from preceding events (e.g., deus ex machina used to produce the dénouement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complication vs dénouement (structural partitioning)
rubrics_metrics.description: The complication comprises events from the beginning up to just before the change of fortune; the dénouement runs from the beginning of the change to the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing or composing, identify the point of change and ensure the preceding entanglement (complication) and the subsequent resolution (dénouement) are both well-handled; many dramatists entangle well but fail at dénouement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: goodness (moral quality relative to class)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should be good (the first and most important point), but 'good' is relative to each class of people (e.g., a woman or a slave may be 'good' relative to their station).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The play shows character by actions and choices; make sure choices presented are good for that class of person. Example: portray people as worthy even while showing faults; avoid gratuitous badness that the plot does not require (example: Menelaos in Orestes as unnecessarily bad).

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: appropriateness (fitting to role)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters must be appropriate — traits must fit the person's social/natural role (e.g., a manly character is not appropriate for a woman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid giving characters abilities, knowledge, or speech inappropriate to their social role (example: Euripides giving Melanippe or female characters inappropriate philosophical knowledge).

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: likeness (verisimilitude)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should be 'like' — plausible and resembling real human types, distinct from merely being good or appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for believable likenesses rather than caricature; render people 'better than themselves' in the poetic sense (as good portrait-painters make likenesses yet improve them).

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: consistency (including 'consistent inconsistency')
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters must be consistent; if the original character in source material is inconsistent, the poet must represent that inconsistency consistently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when depicting changeable or contradictory traits, maintain an internal logic so the audience perceives coherent motivation (example: portray an inconsistent original consistently rather than haphazardly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-drawing: make actions inevitable or probable
rubrics_metrics.description: In character-drawing, one should seek what is inevitable or probable so that it becomes inevitable or probable that a person will say or do a given thing; causes of action should be clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design motivations and causal links so the audience accepts why a character acts; this ensures the plot's incidents follow naturally from character and situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualization and use of gesture (stage imagination)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should keep the scene before his eyes and use gestures to complete effects; imagining the scene as if present helps find what is fitting and detect contradictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to visualize can produce stage incongruities (example: Carcinus making Amphiaraus rise from a temple). Use gestures and visible behaviour to render emotions convincingly; poets should either be impressionable or inspired to do this well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episodes: outline first, then expand; episodes must be appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories should be sketched in outline first and then expanded by inserting episodes; episodes must be appropriate to the main plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In drama episodes are short (they add length in epic but must be concise on stage). Ensure episodes (e.g., madness leading to capture in Orestes) fit and serve the central plot and dénouement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making tragedy an epic (limit scope and multiplicity of stories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not structure a tragedy like an epic composed of many stories; plays that attempt to dramatize whole epic narratives tend to fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the action focused; dramatize a single essential story or episode rather than the entirety of a long saga. Examples of failures: dramatizing the Iliad or Niobe as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus as participant (integrate chorus into action)
rubrics_metrics.description: The chorus must be part of the whole and share in the action — it should function as an actor within the play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid choral odes that have no bearing on the plot (criticised in Euripides). Sophoclean practice models integration of chorus into action; singing interludes unrelated to plot is a fault.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle: a separate, less artistic element
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacle (the visual/spectacular element) is an element of tragedy but is the least artistic of the elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spectacle may contribute but should not substitute for plot or character; do not rely on spectacular display in place of logical incident and emotional justification (e.g., scenes in Hades or grand machinery).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction (modes of speech and elocution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction concerns modes of speech or elocution: commands, prayers, statements, threats, questions, answers, etc.; correct use is part of the poet's craft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know different speech types and their effects; while detailed elocution is subordinate to rhetoric, ignorance of modes of speech is a censure-worthy flaw in dramatic writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (ideas and intended effects of language)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought encompasses what the language is intended to effect: proof and refutation, arousing pity, fear, anger, and so on; these are the rhetorical effects to be achieved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply rules of rhetoric (proof, refutation, arousing emotions, exaggeration, depreciation) to incidents and speeches; some effects should be produced by situation, others by speech. Use speeches to produce effects that would not arise from incidents alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid poet-manufactured revelations and demonstrative proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Revelations or identification scenes concocted purely to 'prove the point' (manufactured declarations) are inartistic compared with discoveries that arise naturally from incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of inartistic practice: characters declaring facts the plot doesn't require (Orestes revealing himself by deliberate speech rather than token), or contrived demonstrations like the 'voice of the shuttle'. Prefer logically caused recognitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deus ex machina ('god in the car') — restricted use
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'god in the car' (deus ex machina) should only be used to explain what lies outside the play (earlier events beyond human knowledge) or to foretell what happens later; it should not be used to produce the dénouement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using a god to 'cut the knot' and declare the dénouement is a weakness (example: Medea's divine carriage spirit away). Reserve machinery for matters outside the dramatic timeframe or for necessary exposition that cannot be otherwise dramatized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre classification: aim to include principal elements
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four varieties/elements of tragedy (reversal/discovery, calamity, character, spectacle); ideally a tragedy should include as many important elements as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While attempting breadth, prioritize achieving the tragic effect (reversal and discovery are central). Modern critics may demand multiple virtues, but the playwright should aim for the combination that best produces pity and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale and tempo: keep dramatic episodes concise
rubrics_metrics.description: In drama episodes are short and serve the central plot; the epic has room for length but tragedies should avoid excessive episodic elongation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose for the stage: long digressions or sprawling subplots are more suited to epic than to tragic performance; keep action tight to maintain emotional effect and probability.
